claims.text: The untreated W–Cu composite suffers from phase segregation and interfacial void formation.
A rapid, liquid-phase-assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering cycle can be applied to a conventional W–Cu composite.
Heating W–Cu briefly to about 2800–3000 K can form a transient eutectic liquid at W/Cu interfaces.
A carbon-based heater can provide the required rapid heating to around 3000 K.
The W–Cu treatment should be performed in an inert or controlled atmosphere.
Fast cooling after the high-temperature dwell will retain a thin, continuous alloyed W–Cu interfacial layer.
The retained interfacial layer will be a W–Cu intermetallic phase or solid solution.
The alloyed interfacial layer will bridge tungsten and copper and act as a binder.
Transient liquid formation promotes interdiffusion and improves wettability at W/Cu interfaces.
The transient liquid heals interfacial voids during W–Cu sintering.
The retained interfacial layer suppresses subsequent W–Cu phase separation.
Reduced void content and improved interfacial bonding improve continuity for phonon and electron transport.
The treated W–Cu composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than an untreated composite.
The treated composite will resist irradiation-induced microstructural degradation better than the untreated composite.
Untreated W–Cu composites have lower thermal conductivity because of phase separation and interfacial voids.
Untreated W–Cu composites perform more poorly under irradiation and thermal cycling.
The intervention is applicable to both discrete W-particle and interconnected W-ligament architectures.
The intervention remains effective under thermal and irradiation loads relevant to plasma-facing joints.
In a high-entropy metal-diboride/boron-carbide composite, rapid heating to around 3000 K formed a small fraction of eutectic liquid at component interfaces.
In that ceramic composite, cooling generated a crystalline dodecaboride intergranular phase that improved adhesion between the components.
